column6: The source commentary centers Allah’s name with Raḥmān/Raḥīm; Exodus has YHWH self-identify as compassionate and gracious, using the Hebrew RḤM cognate in the same divine-name formula.
The commentary links Raḥīm to the womb as a sheltering home; Isaiah asks whether a mother can withhold compassion from the child of her womb, joining the womb image to the RḤM root.
The commentary treats God’s name as a mark identifying the work or creature as belonging to its bearer; the priestly blessing says God’s name is placed on Israel and blesses them.
The commentary connects invoking God’s name with animal offerings; the psalmist makes a thank offering while calling on YHWH’s name, joining liturgical offering and invocation.
The source commentary’s Arabic bism means beginning an act by God’s name; Abram builds an altar and calls in YHWH’s name, a close Hebrew name-invocation formula.
The source labels Allah as the worshipped one and bismillah as name-invocation; Daniel blesses the name of God in Aramaic, using the cognate Elaha for God and linking name, praise, wisdom, and power.
The commentary says expansive mercy does not erase account or judgment; the continuation of the name formula says God forgives while not simply clearing guilt, holding mercy and consequence together.
Jonah cites YHWH’s compassionate, gracious character to explain his flight from the mission; the same RḤM name formula shows mercy reaching even Nineveh, which Jonah resents.
The commentary joins God’s name to mercy and kinship; Jacob asks El Shaddai to grant compassion as his sons travel into danger, with the Hebrew RḤM word directed toward brothers and family.
The source commentary describes mercy through the womb’s care for a helpless child; the true mother’s compassion rises for the living infant and makes her surrender him rather than see him killed.
The commentary presents Rahīm as compassion directed to particular recipients; God speaks of Ephraim as a dear child and says divine compassion is stirred toward him, using the RḤM root.
The commentary distinguishes mercy’s overflowing source from its particular recipients; God says mercy and grace are shown to whom God chooses, with the Hebrew RḤM cognate.
The commentary describes the womb as sustaining a child who cannot ask or repay; the psalm compares YHWH’s compassion to a father’s compassion for children.

column5: The Arabic and Hebrew mercy roots
column6: The commentary’s source label is Arabic ر ح م; Exodus uses Hebrew רַחוּם for God’s compassion. The cognate shows the attribute in its own covenantal declaration, not merely a similar sound.

column5: Sun and moon as objects of worship
column6: The commentary recalls Abraham testing the rising star, moon, and sun and rejecting them when they set; Job names gazing at sun or moon in splendor as the setup for a forbidden act of worship.
The commentary contrasts Allah’s name with a sun treated as divine; Job specifies the hand-kiss that would follow an inwardly enticed heart, making the bodily act of astral devotion explicit.

column5: Worship of celestial bodies as disloyalty
column6: The commentary’s Abraham scene withdraws divine status from a setting star; Job calls sun or moon worship a denial of the God above, supplying the same reversal in an oath.
The commentary distinguishes Allah’s name from empty names assigned to idols; Elijah makes rival groups call on their gods’ names and lets the answer by fire reveal which is truly God.
The commentary contrasts God’s substantial name with names assigned to powerless gods; Isaiah joins YHWH’s self-declared name to refusal to give divine glory to idols.
The commentary says idols are names assigned by people without divine warrant; Jeremiah says the gods that did not make heaven and earth will perish, contrasting them with the Creator.
The commentary cites Aaron warning Israel that the calf is a test and that their Lord is Rahman; Exodus instead has Aaron take their gold and fashion the calf, a sharp difference in the same episode.
The commentary describes Moses returning angry from the calf and throwing down the tablets; Exodus narrates the same action when Moses sees the calf and the dancing.

The commentary presents Aaron warning the people against the calf while Moses challenges him; Exodus has Aaron explain that he cast the gold into the fire and the calf came out, assigning Aaron a different role.

The commentary stresses that Noah’s son refuses the ark and that safety is not inherited by blood; Genesis lists Noah, his sons, and their wives entering, without an estranged son in the passenger scene.
The commentary places the voyage and its beginning under God’s name and mercy; Genesis says YHWH shut Noah in, making divine protection rather than Noah’s invocation the explicit safeguard.
The commentary unpacks Noah’s phrase for the ark’s movement and anchoring as a whole journey under God’s name; Genesis narrates the ark resting on the mountains of Ararat after the flood.
The commentary pairs Noah’s embarkation formula with praise and a request for a blessed landing; after leaving the ark, Genesis has Noah build an altar and offer burnt offerings.
The commentary begins with God’s name and mercy; the Talmud reads Exodus 34:6–7 as a ritual order of divine attributes that Israel can recite when seeking forgiveness.
The commentary reads the Fātiḥa’s opening name as leading into praise, service, and request for guidance; the Talmud says prayer should begin with praise of God before petition.

The commentary says animal flesh and blood do not reach God, but piety does; the psalm says God’s desired sacrifice is a broken and contrite spirit, distinguishing inward devotion from ritual material.
The commentary treats sacrifice as meaningful only under God’s name and with piety; Hosea says God desires steadfast love rather than sacrifice, giving the ethical quality priority over the offering.
The commentary contrasts the animal’s meat and blood with the worshipper’s piety; Micah begins by asking whether burnt offerings and year-old calves can satisfy God.

column5: Thousands of rams do not suffice
column6: The commentary says sacrificial quantity is not what reaches God; Micah escalates to thousands of rams and rivers of oil, then even a firstborn, exposing the insufficiency of material offering.
The commentary identifies piety rather than meat or blood as what reaches God; Micah answers the sacrifice questions with justice, covenant love, and walking humbly with God.
The commentary makes the worshipper’s God-conscious piety decisive; Samuel says listening to YHWH is better than sacrifice and obedience better than sacrificial fat.
The commentary’s brand image says a mark identifies the animal’s owner; Isaiah says God called Israel by name and that Israel belongs to God.

column5: A mark that identifies and protects
column6: The commentary describes a brand as an identifying trace that distinguishes its bearer; Ezekiel marks the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem’s evils so they are spared in judgment.

column5: A divine name on the forehead
column6: The commentary develops the name as an identifying mark; the high priest wears an engraved plate reading holy to YHWH on his forehead while serving with Israel’s offerings.
The commentary says a name raises the named person’s remembrance; God promises to make Abram’s name great, using name for public standing rather than a mere label.
The commentary joins slaughtered animals, a sign, and protection; Exodus directs Israel to put the Passover lamb’s blood on doorposts as a visible sign for the household.

column5: The sign and protection from death
column6: The commentary connects an identifying mark with refuge; Exodus says the blood-marked houses will be passed over when the plague strikes Egypt.
The commentary develops the crescent’s first appearance as a visible time marker and cites pilgrimage timing; Numbers orders trumpet blasts at new moons and festivals as Israel’s calendar signals.
The commentary links mercy to rain that reaches dead ground and brings forth growth; Isaiah compares rain and snow watering earth and making it sprout to God’s life-giving word.
The commentary connects the name formula with conditional speech about future action; James says plans should be stated as what one will do if the Lord wills and one lives.

column5: Every act done in the Lord’s name
column6: The commentary says the missing verb in bismillah is supplied by whatever the speaker is doing; Paul explicitly extends action in the Lord Jesus’ name to every word and deed, with thanksgiving.
The commentary says invocation changes how food is received and used; the letter says every created thing is good when received with thanksgiving to God.
The commentary links naming God with the status of food; the letter says food is sanctified through God’s word and prayer, a Christian meal practice with a different rule from Qur’anic slaughter.
The commentary says meat is not to be eaten when God’s name was not invoked; Paul tells Christians to eat market meat without raising questions of conscience, showing a different criterion.

The commentary makes the invoked name decisive for meat; Paul tells a believer to abstain when someone identifies meat as sacrificial, because of that person’s conscience rather than absence of God’s name.

column5: Eating and drinking for God’s glory
column6: The commentary describes food as transformed by naming God; Paul says eating and drinking alike should be done for God’s glory, giving an explicit Christian frame for ordinary meals.

column5: Prayer begins by hallowing the Name
column6: The commentary says the opening name leads into the Fātiḥa’s praise, service, and request; Jesus’ prayer begins with the Father’s name being hallowed before petitions for provision and forgiveness.

column5: A gift because the recipient bears the Name
column6: The commentary’s brand image identifies who owns the bearer; Jesus promises that a cup of water given because someone belongs to Christ will not lose its reward.

column5: The Name exalted above every name
column6: The commentary explains the name as raised into prominence and uniqueness; Paul says God exalted Jesus and bestowed the name above every name, a Christian confession with a distinct account of divine naming.
The commentary uses Noah’s ark as the refuge in which mercy protects some while others perish; Peter recalls eight people saved through water in Noah’s ark.

The commentary treats entry into Noah’s ark as rescue under divine mercy; Peter interprets the flood’s water typologically through baptism, adding a Christian account of the ark’s saving significance.

The commentary says all who come under Rahman’s mercy are servants, not children of God; Luke’s annunciation calls the child conceived by divine action the Son of God, marking a real difference in theological language.
The commentary says the worshipper’s piety, not sacrificial meat and blood, reaches God; Jesus quotes the prophetic preference for mercy over sacrifice while calling sinners.
The commentary’s stamp image says a name marks who owns the bearer; Revelation depicts the Lamb’s people with his name and his Father’s name written on their foreheads.
The commentary presents Raḥmān and Raḥīm as divine mercy’s source and reach; the psalm repeats the Hebrew RḤM adjective with grace, patience, and abundant steadfast love.

The commentary holds mercy together with reckoning; Moses invokes the compassionate-name formula after Israel’s rebellion and asks God to forgive while the verse also names consequences across generations.
The commentary explains a name as elevated remembrance and good public report; Ecclesiastes says a good name is better than precious oil, treating the name as reputation.

column5: Calling to God during a storm
column6: The commentary places Noah’s ship under God’s name through its motion and rest; the sailors in the psalm cry to YHWH from a storm-tossed ship.
The commentary stresses both the ark’s journey and its anchoring; the psalm says God brings storm-tossed sailors to their desired harbor, a sea-voyage counterpart without making it Noah’s story.
The commentary describes the womb as the child’s protected home and relates its growth to God’s nurturing; the psalm says God formed the speaker in the womb.
The commentary distinguishes overflowing mercy from its direction to individual recipients; the psalm calls YHWH compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, and great in steadfast love.
The commentary reads the divine name as having no namesake or rival; David says there is no God besides YHWH and no one like him.
The commentary develops the question whether God has a namesake or equal; Isaiah says there is no one like God and no other God, a direct theological counterpart.

The commentary connects the unspoken verb of bismillah with whatever work a speaker begins and cites a warning about future plans; James addresses people planning travel, trade, and profit for tomorrow.
The commentary says the work is not self-contained but begins under God’s name; James reminds planners that they do not know what tomorrow brings and that life is brief.

The commentary prohibits meat offered under another god’s name; the Jerusalem decree tells Gentile believers to avoid food sacrificed to idols and blood, preserving a related but differently framed boundary.
The commentary ties the name over an act to its proper religious meaning; Jesus repeats the preference for mercy over sacrifice while defending hungry disciples’ action on the Sabbath.
The commentary pictures mercy as a parent’s active care for a dependent child; the father sees his returning son, is moved with compassion, and runs to embrace him before any repayment.

column5: Mercy belongs to God to give
column6: The commentary distinguishes abundant mercy from its direction to recipients; Paul quotes God’s words to Moses that mercy is shown according to God’s choice, using the same scriptural basis as Exodus 33:19.
The commentary explains a brand as a visible mark identifying the bearer and protecting what is marked; Revelation commands the servants of God to be sealed on their foreheads before judgment.
After declaring the compassionate divine name, Moses asks God to go among Israel, pardon its iniquity, and take it as an inheritance; this makes mercy an active covenantal presence.
Solomon asks God to forgive exiles and grant them compassion before their captors, using the RḤM root; this makes Raḥīm protection concrete for a vulnerable people.
The commentary describes mercy as shelter and as directed care; Moses promises that after exile God will have compassion on Israel and gather the scattered, using the RḤM root.
David chooses to fall into YHWH’s hand because divine mercies are great, rather than into human hands; this links RḤM mercy to the protection and refuge described in the commentary.
The commentary connects Rahman’s name with the Fātiḥa’s request for help; the psalm says Israel’s help is in YHWH’s name, the maker of heaven and earth.

column5: The Name as a safe place
column6: The commentary puts the ark and the womb under the protection of God’s name and mercy; Proverbs says YHWH’s name is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are safe.

column5: The place where God’s Name dwells
column6: The commentary links animals offered at the House with the name spoken over them; Deuteronomy sends Israel to the place God chooses to make his name dwell.

column5: Offerings brought to the named place
column6: The commentary describes animals separated from the herd and brought to the House under God’s name; Deuteronomy lists sacrifices and firstlings brought to the place chosen for YHWH’s name.

column5: A ram offered in place of a son
column6: The commentary considers the status of sacrificial animals and their relation to God; in the binding of Isaac, Abraham offers a ram instead of his son, making the animal’s offering inseparable from a threatened life.

column5: God rejects offerings without right conduct
column6: The commentary says meat and blood do not reach God while piety does; Isaiah has God reject abundant burnt offerings in a community whose worship is disconnected from justice.
The commentary locates the value of offering in the worshipper’s piety; Isaiah turns from rejected sacrifices to washing, ceasing evil, and cleansing conduct.
The commentary says what reaches God is not sacrificial flesh but the worshipper’s God-consciousness; Isaiah specifies justice for the oppressed, orphan, and widow as the required response.
The commentary subordinates sacrificial material to piety; Amos says God will not accept Israel’s burnt offerings and grain offerings in a community facing judgment.
The commentary makes devotion visible in the worshipper rather than the animal’s flesh and blood; Amos follows rejected offerings with a demand that justice flow like water.

The commentary says invoking God’s name changes the status of food; the Mishnah prescribes a blessing before eating different kinds of food, a Jewish table practice that places ordinary eating under God’s name.
The commentary connects God’s name to whether food may be eaten; the Talmud says one may not benefit from the world without a blessing, directly linking invocation to eating.
The commentary’s Raḥmān and Raḥīm name God’s mercy and forgiveness; Sirach says the Lord is compassionate and merciful, forgives sins, and saves in distress.

The commentary distinguishes overflowing mercy from its direction to recipients; Sirach contrasts human compassion for a neighbor with the Lord’s compassion for all living beings and a shepherd’s care for the flock.
The commentary says divine mercy encompasses everything; Wisdom says God has mercy on all because God can do all things and patiently allows sinners to repent.

column5: Creation belongs to its merciful Lord
column6: The commentary links the name with mercy toward creatures; Wisdom says God spares all because all are God’s, adding belonging to universal mercy.
The commentary holds mercy together with judgment; Nehemiah’s communal confession recalls rebellion and calls God ready to pardon, gracious, and merciful, using the RḤM formula.

The commentary describes expansive mercy that does not erase moral reckoning; Joel uses the compassionate-name formula to call Israel to return, with God’s relenting from calamity as the hoped-for response.
The commentary says Raḥīm turns toward particular people; Hezekiah promises that returning exiles’ kin may find compassion because YHWH is gracious and merciful and will not turn away.
The commentary joins mercy to God’s name and care for those under it; Moses says YHWH is a merciful God who will not abandon Israel or forget the covenant, using the RḤM root.

column5: A deed begun in YHWH’s Name
column6: The commentary says the speaker puts God’s name before the action; David tells Goliath that he comes against him in the name of YHWH, making the name the declared authority for a concrete deed.
The commentary opens with God’s name and leads into praise; Mary’s song says the Mighty One has done great things and his name is holy, placing the Name in a liturgical act of thanksgiving.
The commentary joins God’s name with mercy; Mary’s song immediately describes mercy extending through generations to those who fear God, making the two themes part of one praise sequence.
The commentary treats God’s name as a mark that identifies and claims the bearer; Jesus commands baptism into the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, a Christian ritual that marks belonging.

column5: Communion limited to the baptized in the Name
column6: The commentary links God’s name to food’s religious status; the Didache says only the baptized into the Lord’s name may eat or drink the Eucharist, making the Name a boundary for a sacred meal.

column5: Thanksgiving for the holy Name at the meal
column6: The commentary places food and praise under God’s name; the Didache’s post-meal thanksgiving blesses God for the holy Name made to dwell in believers’ hearts.
The commentary says the divine name accompanies a concrete action; Peter tells the lame man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ, making the Name the stated means of the act.

column5: Calling on the Lord’s Name for rescue
column6: The commentary connects God’s name with seeking help and protection; Peter quotes Joel that everyone who calls on the Lord’s name will be saved, applying the invocation to deliverance.

column5: The one who comes in the Lord’s Name
column6: The commentary describes the Name at the threshold of a journey and cites a letter identified by sender and divine Name; the crowd welcomes Jesus with the scriptural blessing for the one who comes in the Lord’s name.
The commentary distinguishes piety from animal flesh and blood; Peter describes believers as a priesthood offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
The commentary reads rain and fruitful earth as signs of mercy that feed life; Paul says God gave rain, fruitful seasons, food, and gladness as testimony to divine goodness.
The commentary contrasts God’s living name with human-assigned empty divine names; Paul says an idol is nothing and that there is no God but one.
The commentary keeps Rahman’s mercy in view alongside the Day of Judgment; James says mercy triumphs over judgment, making mercy’s role at judgment explicit.

The commentary presents Harun warning Israel rather than endorsing the calf; Rashi reads Aaron’s announcement of a festival “tomorrow” as an attempt to delay the people until Moses returned, mitigating Aaron’s role in the parallel episode.

column5: Mercy invoked by an individual petitioner
column6: The commentary describes Raḥīm as compassion directed toward a recipient; the psalmist calls on the merciful, gracious, patient God while asking for personal mercy and rescue.
The commentary presents Rahman’s mercy as encompassing creation; the psalm says YHWH is good to all and has compassion over all his works.
The commentary says the missing verb in bismillah is supplied by the act being undertaken; Moses tells God he has spoken to Pharaoh in God’s name, a specific speech act placed under the Name.

column5: A people publicly identified by the Name
column6: The commentary’s brand image makes a mark identify its bearer; Deuteronomy says the nations will see that Israel is called by YHWH’s name and fear them.

column5: Stars as created signs, not gods
column6: The commentary recalls Abraham considering the star, moon, and sun as possible lords before rejecting them; Genesis has God point to the stars as a promise of descendants, giving celestial bodies a created sign-function instead of divine status.

The commentary connects Raḥīm with the womb and bodily care; Luke speaks of the tender compassion of God using an inward-organ image, then pictures dawn visiting from on high. The Greek image is a motif, not a cognate.
The commentary connects invocation and food; the Didache begins its Eucharistic thanksgiving over the cup, showing a communal meal opened by blessing and gratitude.

column5: The worshipper as a living offering
column6: The commentary says piety, rather than meat and blood, reaches God; Paul calls believers to present their bodies as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice, making devotion itself the offering.

column5: Praise as a sacrifice of the lips
column6: The commentary’s opening name leads into praise and service; Hebrews calls continual praise, confessing God’s name, a sacrifice offered through Jesus.

The commentary says sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God, while piety does; Hebrews says animal blood cannot take away sins and directs its argument toward Christ’s offering, a different account of sacrifice’s efficacy.
The commentary says Allah’s name identifies the sole one worthy of worship; Paul confesses one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, while distinguishing the Christian formulation.
The commentary describes compassion as active kindness toward the vulnerable; Jesus blesses the merciful with the promise that they will receive mercy.

column5: Mercy not earned by human effort
column6: The commentary says sacrificial material does not reach God but piety does; Paul’s continuation says mercy does not depend on human willing or running but on God’s mercy, a distinct account of agency and merit.
